title: MMLongBench-Doc: Benchmarking Long-context Document Understanding with Visualizations
research_question: How well can current vision-language and language models understand long multimodal documents when answering questions that require evidence localization, cross-page reasoning, multiple document modalities, and resistance to hallucination?
methodology: The authors construct MMLongBench-Doc from 135 PDF documents spanning seven document types and annotate 1,082 question-answer pairs with reference answers, evidence pages, evidence-source modalities, and answer formats. Questions cover text, layout, tables, charts, and images, and include single-page, cross-page, and deliberately unanswerable cases. Fourteen LVLMs are evaluated from page screenshots and ten LLMs from OCR-parsed text, using response generation followed by GPT-4o answer extraction and rule-based scoring with generalized accuracy and F1. A subset is also evaluated by humans for comparison.

key_findings.finding: The benchmark explicitly preserves page-level provenance and evidence-source type for answers, covering text, layout, tables, charts, and images.
key_findings.section: 3.2 Question and Answer Collection; 3.4 Dataset Overview and Analysis

key_findings.finding: Long-document understanding remains difficult: the best evaluated LVLM, GPT-4o, achieves 44.9% overall F1, compared with a 66.0% human F1 baseline.

Cross-page questions are substantially represented and models generally perform worse on cross-page than single-page questions, demonstrating difficulty gathering and reasoning over evidence distributed across pages.
key_findings.section: 3.4 Dataset Overview and Analysis; 4.4 Fine-grained Results

key_findings.finding: Most evaluated LVLMs perform worse than LLM counterparts supplied with lossy OCR text, although GPT-4o and GPT-4V are exceptions.

OCR-based LLM pipelines are competitive on text and table questions but comparatively weak on chart- and image-dependent questions, showing that flattening documents to text can discard important multimodal evidence.
Model performance generally declines as answer evidence occurs later in a document, indicating that evidence location within a long context materially affects retrieval and answering performance.
The inclusion of unanswerable questions allows the benchmark to evaluate whether models produce unsupported answers when no evidence exists in the document.

limitations: The benchmark is relatively small, containing 135 documents and 1,082 questions, because expert annotation of long documents is expensive.
The benchmark uses only a coarse single-page, cross-page, and unanswerable taxonomy rather than a detailed taxonomy of perception and reasoning capabilities.

Evidence localization is primarily represented at page level plus evidence-source category; it does not generally provide cell-, bounding-region-, or object-level provenance suitable for precise source reconstruction.
The automatic evaluation pipeline depends on GPT-4o to extract short answers from model responses before rule-based scoring, introducing an additional model-dependent evaluation stage.
The benchmark evaluates documents as a static collection and does not model attachment revisions or version-relative provenance.
raw_claims: MMLongBench-Doc contains 135 lengthy PDF documents and 1,082 annotated questions.
The documents average about 47.5 pages and roughly 21,214 textual tokens.
Answer evidence is annotated across text, layout, table, chart, and image sources.
There are 365 cross-page questions and 223 unanswerable questions in the reported benchmark version.
Each answerable question is associated with one or more evidence pages.
GPT-4o obtains 44.9% overall F1 in the reported evaluation.
The human evaluation produces an overall F1 of 66.0%.
Most LVLMs evaluated on document images perform worse than LLM counterparts using OCR text.
Models tend to perform better when evidence appears near the beginning of a document.
Cross-page questions are consistently more difficult than single-page questions for the evaluated models.
